series.name: Private rents index (IPHRP)
series.source: ONS Index of Private Housing Rental Prices

discontinuities.note: IPHRP was discontinued in March 2025 and replaced by the Price Index of Private Rents (PIPR); the final year is a partial one
Transition from the Labour Force Survey to the Transformed LFS changes the basis

series.name: Average weekly earnings (total pay)
notes: Whole-economy seasonally adjusted total pay, mean not median; the series starts in 2000

series.name: Public sector debt interest
notes: Interest and dividends paid to the private sector and rest of world, excluding public sector banks

series.name: Public sector net debt
notes: Excluding public sector banks

discontinuities.note: Attendance recording rules and school opening changed; the series is not comparable across this point
No KS2 assessments in 2019/20 and 2020/21; the gap on either side is not measured on identical cohorts

series.name: Net migration (LTIM)

discontinuities.note: ONS moved from the International Passenger Survey to an administrative-data method; estimates before and after are not produced the same way, and the series only starts in 2012 on the current basis

notes: Each point is the year ending December, taken from a rolling four-quarter series
The most recent years are provisional and have been revised substantially in the past — YE June 2024 was first published at 906,000 and now stands well below that

series.name: Small boat arrivals
notes: Detections only. This is not a count of everyone who entered without permission, and the Home Office says so explicitly
The final year is partial — the release covers quarters up to the year ending March 2026

series.name: Asylum cases awaiting an initial decision
notes: A stock, not a flow — the number of claims sitting undecided at the end of the year, so it falls when decisions speed up as well as when claims fall
Excludes cases pending further review, which are counted separately

series.name: Asylum grant rate at initial decision
notes: Main applicants only. Withdrawn and administrative outcomes are excluded from both halves of the fraction
Initial decisions only — it says nothing about what happens on appeal, where a large share of refusals are overturned

series.name: Asylum seekers in hotel accommodation
notes: The population in hotels, not the bill. Hotel SPEND is only published in the Home Office annual report and accounts, as a PDF, so it cannot be fetched — see the aid-funded refugee-cost series for the part of it that is machine-readable
Hotel is identified separately only from December 2022; earlier hotel use is inside a combined Section 98 category

series.name: Enforced removals
notes: Enforced returns only. Voluntary returns are the larger number and are counted separately — quoting either alone overstates or understates the total

series.name: Study visas granted
series.source: Home Office entry clearance visa statistics
notes: Main applicants and dependants combined

series.name: Study visas granted to dependants
series.source: Home Office entry clearance visa statistics
notes: Dependants of students went from roughly 13,000 a year to 143,000 in three years, then collapsed after the January 2024 rule change. Almost nobody predicts this line correctly

series.name: Work visas granted
series.source: Home Office entry clearance visa statistics

series.name: Health and Care Worker visas granted
series.source: Home Office entry clearance visa statistics
notes: A route created in August 2020. It went from nothing to the single largest work route and back down again inside five years, entirely through policy decisions

series.name: Overseas aid as a share of national income
notes: The 0.7% target was met from 2013 to 2020 and cut to 0.5% in 2021
The ratio has been propped up since 2022 by aid spent inside the UK on refugees, which counts as ODA under OECD rules — see the in-donor refugee cost series

series.name: Aid spent on refugees inside the UK
notes: This is the machine-readable slice of asylum accommodation spend: the aid budget charged for housing asylum seekers in the UK, most of it Home Office hotel costs
It peaked at 28% of the entire aid budget in 2022

series.name: Payments to EU institutions, gross
notes: Total UK payments to EU institutions, after the rebate is deducted. The rebate was never actually sent — it came off the bill at source — which is why the £350m a week figure, which added it back on, was never money that could have been spent elsewhere

series.name: Receipts from EU institutions
notes: Money coming back — farm payments, structural funds, research grants. The gap between this and the gross payment is the net contribution

series.name: Net position with EU institutions
notes: Negative means the UK paid in more than it got back

series.name: Non-domiciled taxpayers
notes: Individuals rounded to the nearest 100 by HMRC
Non-dom status was abolished from April 2025, so this series ends as a measure of the old regime

series.name: Tax and NICs paid by non-domiciled taxpayers
notes: Liabilities, not receipts, and it is the total tax these people pay — not a measure of what the non-dom regime costs, which is a different and much harder number

series.name: Foreign nationals in prison
notes: The population as at 30 June each year, both sexes, all custody types
A count, not a share. It has been roughly flat at ten to eleven thousand for a decade while the prison population itself moved, so the percentage and the number tell different stories

series.name: Crime Survey estimate of crime
series.source: ONS Crime in England and Wales

discontinuities.note: Face-to-face interviewing stopped during the pandemic; the telephone survey that replaced it is not comparable, so there is a genuine hole here rather than a zero

notes: Asks people what happened to them, so it counts crime whether or not it was reported. This is the series that shows crime falling by around two thirds since the mid-1990s
Excludes fraud and computer misuse, which would otherwise dominate the total

series.name: Police recorded crime
series.source: ONS Crime in England and Wales (Home Office police recorded crime)

discontinuities.note: A change in recording practice following HMIC inspections; the rise from here on is substantially a recording effect rather than a change in crime

notes: Counts what the police wrote down. It rose sharply from 2014 largely because forces were told to record crime properly after being found not to be, which is why it moves opposite to the survey
Not accredited as official statistics, on those grounds

series.name: Charge rate, all offences
series.source: Home Office Crime Outcomes in England and Wales
notes: The share of recorded offences that ended in someone being charged or summonsed. It fell by roughly two thirds between 2014-15 and 2021-22 before recovering slightly

series.name: Charge rate, violence against the person
series.source: Home Office police recorded crime and outcomes open data
notes: Measured against the offences recorded in the same period, which is the basis the headline charge rate uses. The most recent year is therefore understated — a lot of those investigations are still open, and their outcomes get assigned later

That lag is not even across offence types. Sexual offences take the longest to investigate, so they are depressed the most in the latest year: on the closed-investigations basis the same year reads roughly twice as high

series.name: Road deaths
notes: Deaths reported to the police on the STATS19 form. Fatalities are near-completely reported, so this is the most reliable series in the road safety set
The 1926 start predates driving tests, MOTs and speed limits on most roads; deaths peaked in 1966 at over 7,900 with a fraction of today's traffic

series.name: Road casualties, all severities
notes: Police-reported casualties only. DfT says plainly that non-fatal injuries are substantially under-reported — comparison with survey and hospital data suggests a large share never reaches a STATS19 form — so treat the level as a floor and the trend as the useful part
Slight-injury counts are also affected by forces changing their injury-reporting systems from 2016, which raised recorded severity without any change on the road

series.name: Road traffic
notes: The denominator the casualty figures should usually be read against: traffic has roughly quadrupled since 1950 while deaths have fallen by around three quarters

series.name: Local bus passenger journeys
notes: Years ending March, so the year labelled 2021 is the one the pandemic hit hardest — journeys roughly halved and have not returned to the 2005 level

series.name: Renewable share of electricity generation
series.publisher_full: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
notes: Share of electricity *generated*, not of energy consumed. Electricity is roughly a fifth of UK final energy use, so a renewables share above half does not mean half the country's energy is renewable
Includes biomass, which is counted as renewable in this series but is contested as a carbon-neutral fuel

series.name: Low-carbon share of electricity generation
series.publisher_full: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
notes: Renewables plus nuclear. Overlaps the renewables series rather than adding to it

series.name: Fossil fuel share of electricity generation
series.publisher_full: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
notes: Coal, oil and gas. Coal's share went from around a third of generation in 1998 to nil when the last coal plant closed in 2024, so most of what remains here is gas

series.name: Active businesses
notes: The starting point for demography is the concept of a population of active businesses in a reference year (t). These are defined as businesses that had either turnover or employment at any time during the reference period.

series.name: Business births
notes: A birth is identified as a business that was present in year t, but did not exist in year t-1 or t-2. Births are identified by making comparison of annual active population files and identifying those present in the latest file, but not the two previous ones.
The birth rate is calculated using the number of births as a proportion of the active businesses.

series.name: Business deaths
notes: A death is defined as a business that was on the active file in year t, but was no longer present in the active file in t+1 and t+2. In order to provide an early estimate of deaths, an adjustment has been made to the latest two years deaths to allow for reactivations. These figures are provisional and subject to revision.
The death rate is calculated using the number of deaths as a proportion of the active businesses.

series.name: Claimant Count
notes: Not the unemployment rate: it counts benefit claims, which respond to eligibility rules as well as to the labour market. Read it against the LFS unemployment series rather than instead of it
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development
Proportions of people claiming are the number of claimants in a year divided by the population aged from 16 to 64 from mid-year 2023 population estimates.

The experimental Claimant Count consists of claimants of Jobseekers Allowance (JSA) and some Universal Credit (UC) Claimants. The UC claimants that are included are 1) those that were recorded as not in employment (May 2013-April 2015), and 2) those claimants of Universal Credit who are required to search for work, i.e. within the Searching for Work conditionality regime as defined by the Department for Work & Pensions (from April 2015 onwards).
The count is based on live claims on the second Thursday of the reference month.

Under certain circumstances, some people are able to claim both contribution-based JSA and UC at the same time. Consequently, there has been a small amount of double counting. Information from DWP suggests this double counting increased at the start of the pandemic and has stabilised at approximately 1.0 to 1.5% of the Claimant Count.
Northern Ireland local government districts Claimant Count figures are only available from 2013 onwards.

series.name: Economic inactivity rate
notes: ONS titles this indicator Great Britain but serves the top-level row as 'United Kingdom'. Published here on the narrower claim in the title
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development

Calculation of economic inactivity rate: number of economically inactive people aged 16 to 64 years divided by the population aged 16 to 64 years. Population is the sum of employed plus unemployed plus inactive.

The ongoing challenges with response rates, response levels and weighting approach mean that labour market statistics based on both the Labour Force Survey (LFS) and Annual Population Survey (APS) will be considered [official statistics in development](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/policies/official-statistics-policies/official-statistics-in-development/) until further review. Because of increased volatility of LFS and APS estimates, estimates of change should be treated with additional caution.
Updates to this indicator have been temporarily suspended until the APS reweighting is implemented in 2026.

series.name: Employment rate
notes: ONS titles this indicator Great Britain but serves the top-level row as 'United Kingdom'. Published here on the narrower claim in the title
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development
Calculation of employment rate: number of employed people aged 16 to 64 years divided by the population aged 16 to 64 years. Population is the sum of employed plus unemployed plus inactive.

The ongoing challenges with response rates, response levels and weighting approach mean that labour market statistics based on both the Labour Force Survey (LFS) and Annual Population Survey (APS) will be considered [official statistics in development](https://osr.statisticsauthority.gov.uk/policies/official-statistics-policies/official-statistics-in-development/) until further review. Because of increased volatility of LFS and APS estimates, estimates of change should be treated with additional caution.
Updates to this indicator have been temporarily suspended until the APS reweighting is implemented in 2026.

series.name: Food outlets
notes: The data for this indicator is sourced from [Nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/query/construct/summary.asp?reset=yes&mode=construct&dataset=142&version=0), based on an extract from the Inter-Departmental Business Register (IDBR). This dataset records the number of enterprises that were live at a reference point in March each year.

An enterprise can be thought of as the overall business, made up of all the individual sites or workplaces. It is defined as the smallest combination of legal units (generally based on VAT and/or PAYE records) that has a certain degree of autonomy within an enterprise group.

Please refer to the [UK business; activity, size and location quality and methods guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/businessindustryandtrade/business/activitysizeandlocation/methodologies/ukbusinessactivitysizeandlocationqmi) for more information.

Mid-year population estimates for the period 2010 to 2024 have been used to calculate rates per 1,000 population (sourced from [Nomis](https://www.nomisweb.co.uk/datasets/pestsyoala)). The most recent (2024) population estimates have been used to produce rates for the 2025 data.

series.name: Gross disposable household income per head
notes: Figures for 2023 are provisional, as national estimates have not been through supply and use balancing at the time of the data source publication.

series.name: Gross domestic product per head in chained volume measures
notes: Chained volume measures — real terms, and the series to use for 'are we better off', with the cash series alongside to show how much of the nominal rise was prices

This time series has the effects of inflation removed by considering changes in quantity between consecutive periods, holding prices from previous periods constant and is most useful for monitoring growth over time within any given area.
2023 data are provisional.

Data for the City of London has been excluded from the visualisations on this service due to its very high GDP figures and very low population, which distort the overall representation. Please refer to the accompanying dataset below or the [data source](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossdomesticproductgdp/bulletins/regionaleconomicactivitybygrossdomesticproductuk/previousreleases) for this information.

series.name: Gross domestic product per head at current market prices
notes: Cash prices, so most of the rise before the mid-2000s is inflation. The chained volume series is the real-terms answer to the same question
This time series includes the effects of inflation and is most useful for comparison of levels between different areas.
2023 data are provisional.

Data for the City of London has been excluded from the visualisations on this service due to its very high GDP figures and very low population, which distort the overall representation. Please refer to the accompanying dataset below or the [data source](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/grossdomesticproductgdp/bulletins/regionaleconomicactivitybygrossdomesticproductuk/previousreleases) for this information.

series.name: Gross median weekly pay
notes: The median, and residence-based — the existing average weekly earnings series is a workplace-based mean over a different population, so the two are not alternative estimates of the same thing and the gap between them is the point
Assembled by ONS from more than one collection (Office for National Statistics, Northern Ireland Statistics and Research Agency), so the nations are not always on identical definitions

For Great Britain data, 2025 estimates are provisional and relate to the pay period that includes 30 April 2025. Estimates for 2024 have been revised and relate to the pay period that includes 17 April 2024.
The country level figure for Northern Ireland has been sourced from Nomis rather than NISRA. This is to allow for confidence intervals.

Combined Authority data has been sourced from the following: [2023 (revised)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/adhocs/2934annualsurveyofhoursandearningsestimatesofearningsofresidencebasedemployeesbycombinedauthorities), [2024 (revised) and 2025 (provisional)](https://www.ons.gov.uk/employmentandlabourmarket/peopleinwork/earningsandworkinghours/adhocs/3107annualsurveyofhoursandearningsestimatesofearningsofresidenceandworkbasedemployeesbycombinedauthorities2024revisedand2025provisional).

series.name: High growth businesses
notes: High growth measures all businesses with an average growth in employment of greater than 20%, per annum, over a three-year period. The size threshold used to identify these businesses is that they have 10 or more employees.
The rate of high growth businesses is calculated using the number of high growth businesses as a proportion of the active businesses with 10 or more employees.

series.name: Inward foreign direct investment
notes: Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development

Foreign direct investment (FDI) is cross-border investment made with the objective of establishing a lasting interest in the host economy. FDI is also defined by control relationships, where the direct investor (parent company) controls at least 10% of the voting power (ordinary shares) of the direct investment enterprise. These relationships can be measured in two directions:
- outward: the direct investments of UK-resident companies in other countries.
- inward: the direct investments in the UK from non-resident companies.

Several factors affected FDI statistics for 2020. This not only includes disruption from the coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic and global recession, but also some changes to the FDI statistical populations and sampling methods. We advise caution when comparing results for 2020 with earlier years. More detail can be found in [Foreign direct investment statistics, overview of methods changes: 2020](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/nationalaccounts/balanceofpayments/articles/foreigndirectinvestmentstatisticsoverviewofmethodschanges/2020).

series.name: Air pollution regulating
notes: A valuation of an ecosystem service, not spending: ONS estimates what the vegetation's removal of air pollutants would otherwise have cost in health damage. Treat it as an accounting estimate with wide uncertainty, not a measured flow of money
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development
This data includes all pollutants and all habitats.

Please refer to the [UK natural capital accounts quality and methods guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/methodologies/uknaturalcapitalaccountsqualityandmethodsguide) for more information.

series.name: Greenhouse gas emissions
series.publisher_full: Department for Energy Security and Net Zero
notes: Greenhouse gas emissions (tCO2e) per capita refers to the average amount of greenhouse gas emissions produced by each person in a specific area over a year. This metric is calculated by dividing the total greenhouse gas emissions of an area by its population. The result is expressed in tonnes of CO2 equivalent (tCO2e) per person.
Greenhouse gas emissions here include territorial emissions of carbon dioxide (CO2), methane (CH4) and nitrous oxide (N2O).

Emissions are reported against the areas where they occurred except for emissions associated with energy supply that are distributed to the areas based on where the 'end-use' of the energy occurred and emissions from waste that have been distributed based on the waste arising in each area.
Emissions data is from UK local authority greenhouse gas emissions estimates where some emissions can't be fully allocated to individual local authorities for technical or disclosure reasons.
Some of this data has been aggregated and may show differences to other published figures.
Emissions data is also visualised on [Local Authority Greenhouse Gas Map.](https://naei.energysecurity.gov.uk/laghgapp/)

series.name: Greenhouse gas regulating
notes: A valuation of carbon sequestration by UK habitats, priced at the government's non-traded carbon values. Not money that changed hands
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development
This data includes all habitats.
Local greenhouse gas regulating estimates are produced through local authority modelling of national estimates and are not specific to the land management of each authority.
Greenhouse gas regulating estimates measure the net greenhouse gas emitted and absorbed.

Please refer to the [UK natural capital accounts quality and methods guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/methodologies/uknaturalcapitalaccountsqualityandmethodsguide) for more information.

series.name: Urban heat regulating
notes: A valuation of the cooling urban vegetation provides. Not money that changed hands
England only. ONS's own metadata lists this indicator as UK-wide, but no UK-level figure is served
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development
Hot days are defined as days with a maximum temperature of 28 degrees Celsius and above.
The UK and country level values for the number of hot days are the sum of the number of hot days per local authority.

There are two parts to the calculation of annual value. The value that nature provides in work productivity savings during hot days and savings on air conditioning. The air conditioning value is based on a model from 2014 and we assume a flat time series for this contribution. When there are no hot days for a local authority, this means that the only value comes from the air conditioning value.

These values have been rounded to 1 decimal place. Some Local Authorities with 0 values may have an annual and asset value that are hidden by being rounded to 1 decimal place. Please view the Natural Capital Accounts [Detailed Summary Tables](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/datasets/uknaturalcapitalaccountsdetailedsummarytables) for the full details.

Please refer to the [UK natural capital accounts quality and methods guide](https://www.ons.gov.uk/economy/environmentalaccounts/methodologies/uknaturalcapitalaccountsqualityandmethodsguide) for more information.

series.name: Female healthy life expectancy
notes: Healthy life expectancy, not life expectancy — years lived in self-reported good health. It has been flat or falling while total life expectancy rose, which is the whole reason to plot the two together
Pooled 2-year estimates, plotted at the first year of each band — a point here summarises 2 years, not one
Published by ONS as an experimental statistic — the method is still under development

Healthy life expectancy is a summary measure of health that adds a quality dimension to estimates of life expectancy by dividing expected lifespan into time spent in different states of health. Healthy life expectancy measures health-related wellbeing and represents the average time an individual is expected to live in "very good" or "good" general health, based on how individuals perceive their general health.

The estimates in this indicator have been produced using an interim methodological fix. The decline in sample size of the Annual Population Survey has impaired our ability to continue using the previous method to estimate age-specific prevalence of "good" general health by local authority. We therefore used logistic regression to estimate "good" health prevalence instead of using the survey's observed prevalence. This enables continuity in local area reporting with a viable, comparable time series. ONS is currently conducting a review of data sources to assess their future potential to provide robust, reliable and durable measures of health status.
Figures are based on the number of deaths registered, mid-year population estimates, and health state prevalence aggregated over three consecutive years. Figures exclude deaths of non-residents.
Estimates for Isles of Scilly and City of London are excluded because of insufficient population counts.
Estimates for Northern Ireland’s local government districts are available only from 2014 to 2016 onward.

These estimates of healthy life expectancy in Northern Ireland use different methods and data sources compared to those produced by the Northern Ireland Department of Health; please see their [Health inequalities annual report](https://www.health-ni.gov.uk/news/health-inequalities-annual-report-2025) for more information.

More quality and methodology information on strengths, limitations, appropriate uses, and how the data were created is available in the [Health state life expectancies, UK quality and methodology information (QMI) report](https://www.ons.gov.uk/peoplepopulationandcommunity/healthandsocialcare/healthandlifeexpectancies/methodologies/healthstatelifeexpectanciesukqmi2020to2022).

series.name: Average house price
notes: For the UK House Price Index (UK HPI), the standard average house price is calculated by taking the average (geometric mean) price in January 2015 and then recalculating it in accordance with the index change back in time and forward to the present day. The geometric mean reduces the weighting given to high value properties when compared to the arithmetic mean and is typically lower, usually closer to that of the median.

Estimates for the most recent months are provisional and are likely to be updated as more data is incorporated into the index. Read [Revisions to the UK HPI data](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/about-the-uk-house-price-index/about-the-uk-house-price-index#monthly-revision).

The UK House Price Index (UK HPI) is calculated by the Office for National Statistics and Land & Property Services Northern Ireland. Find out about the [methodology used](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/about-the-uk-house-price-index/quality-and-methodology#methods-used-to-produce-the-uk-hpi) to create the UK HPI.

Data for the UK House Price Index is provided by HM Land Registry, Registers of Scotland, The Land & Property Services Northern Ireland Statistics & Research Agency and the Valuation Office Agency. Find out more [about the UK House Price Index](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/about-the-uk-house-price-index).

series.name: First-time buyer mortgage sales
notes: Mortgage Product Sales Data (PSD001) is regulatory data reported to the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) by regulated mortgage lenders.
This data reflects the number of mortgages taken out by first-time buyers, either individually or jointly, but does not include first-time buyers who purchased a property without a mortgage.

The first-time buyer indicator in the FCA data is reported by the mortgage providers and its definition may vary across firms. For example, for individuals who are not remortgaging but have previously owned a property may or may not be counted as first-time buyers. Additionally, if a mortgage is taken out jointly by one first-time buyer and one non-first-time buyer, it may or may not be counted as a first-time buyer.
The dwelling stock estimates used are published by MHCLG, Welsh Government, Scottish Government and the Northern Ireland Department of Finance.

Some of this data has been aggregated and may differ from other published figures. Data for the Isles of Scilly is unavailable for all years due to low counts. Mortgage sales for Isles of Scilly have been excluded from aggregated areas that would normally include data from this area.

series.name: Five-year population change
notes: Population estimates in Explore Local Statistics (ELS) are informed by those available on Nomis at the time of publication on ELS.

series.name: Median age
notes: Median age is calculated as the age category in which the mid-point of the population distribution falls. There may be slight differences when compared with other sources, as these may reflect where the mid-point falls within the given age category. These reflect differences in precision, not accuracy.
Population estimates in Explore Local Statistics (ELS) are informed by those available on Nomis at the time of publication on ELS.

Data on ELS will be updated when the [Population estimates for the UK, England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland: mid-2025](https://www.ons.gov.uk/releases/populationestimatesfortheukenglandwalesscotlandandnorthernirelandmid2025) release is published, provisionally scheduled for September to October 2026.
